unit.name: Interpreting Results & The Statistical Enquiry Cycle
unit.subtitle: Reading correlation, judging conclusions, and walking through the full Statistical Enquiry Cycle from question to review.

lessons.title: Correlation, Causation and the Vocabulary of Association
lessons.description: Reading scatter relationships using the full correlation vocabulary, and why association is not the same as cause.
lessons.content_html:
What Is Correlation?

When two variables tend to change together, we say there is a correlation between them. Correlation is about pattern, not proof. Statisticians have a precise vocabulary for describing correlations, and using the right term in the right context is one of the most reliable ways to pick up marks in interpretation questions.

Direction: Positive, Negative and Zero

Positive correlation means that as one variable increases, the other tends to increase too. Hours of revision and exam score typically show positive correlation: students who revise more tend to score higher.

Negative correlation means that as one variable increases, the other tends to decrease. Distance from the city centre and house price often show negative correlation: properties further from the centre tend to cost less (though this depends heavily on context).

Zero correlation (no correlation) means there is no consistent relationship between the two variables. The points on a scatter graph are scattered randomly with no discernible pattern.

Key Fact

The three directions: positive correlation (both variables increase together), negative correlation (one increases as the other decreases), zero correlation (no consistent pattern). The word “moderate” for correlation strength is NOT used in this specification — use strong, weak, or no correlation only.

Strength: Strong, Weak and No Correlation

The strength of a correlation describes how closely the points cluster around a straight line. The specification defines precise thresholds for strength based on the value of the correlation coefficient \(r\):

  • Strong correlation: \(|r| \geq 0.6\) (i.e. \(r \geq 0.6\) or \(r \leq -0.6\))
  • Weak correlation: \(0.2 \leq |r| < 0.6\) (i.e. between 0.2 and 0.6 in magnitude)
  • No correlation: \(|r| < 0.2\) (i.e. between \(-0.2\) and \(0.2\), not including these endpoints)

These thresholds are fixed by the specification. Do not use the word “moderate” — the specification explicitly excludes this term. Do not make up your own thresholds. Use strong, weak, or no correlation as described above.

Interpolation and Extrapolation

Interpolation means using the line of best fit to estimate a value that falls within the range of the data you collected. If your data covers ages 20 to 60 and you estimate for age 35, that is interpolation. Interpolation is generally considered reliable when the correlation is strong.

Extrapolation means extending the line beyond the range of your data to estimate a value. If your data covers ages 20 to 60 and you try to estimate for age 80, that is extrapolation. Extrapolation is much less reliable — the relationship seen within the data range may not continue outside it. The line of best fit might predict a negative house price if extended far enough, which is obviously impossible.

Key Fact

Interpolation (within the data range) is generally more reliable. Extrapolation (beyond the data range) is risky because the relationship seen in the data may not continue outside it. The further you extrapolate, the less reliable the estimate.

Causation vs Association

This is the most important idea in this lesson — and one of the most commonly examined. Finding a strong correlation between two variables does NOT mean that one causes the other. The specification explicitly states: correlation does not necessarily imply causation.

Consider this: there is a strong positive correlation between ice cream sales and drowning incidents over time. Does ice cream cause drowning? No. Both variables share a common cause: hot weather. People buy more ice cream in hot weather, and more people swim in hot weather, leading to more drowning incidents. The ice cream and the drowning are both responses to the temperature — they did not cause each other.

The hidden factor that explains both variables is called a lurking variable (also called a confounding variable). The specification says you should know that there are multiple factors that may interact. Any time you see a strong correlation, a good statistician asks: “Is there a third variable that could explain this?”

This is one of the most tested misconceptions in GCSE Statistics. Students see a correlation of 0.8 and write “the increase in X causes an increase in Y.” This will cost marks.

The correct language is: “There is a strong positive correlation between X and Y. This suggests X and Y are associated, but this does not mean X causes Y. There could be a lurking variable that explains both.” Using the word “associated” rather than “causes” shows the examiner you understand the distinction.

Interpreting Spearman's Rank and Pearson's PMCC (Higher)

At Higher tier, you need to interpret calculated values of two correlation coefficients. Spearman's rank correlation coefficient measures the strength and direction of correlation between the rank orders of two variables — not the raw values. It works for any data that can be ranked, including ordinal data.

Pearson's product moment correlation coefficient (PMCC) measures the strength and direction of a linear relationship between two quantitative variables. The key distinction: Spearman's measures correlation of rank orders, whereas Pearson's measures the linear relationship itself. For a straight-line relationship between continuous variables, Pearson's is more appropriate; for ranked or ordinal data, Spearman's is preferred.

The formula for Spearman's rank will always be given in the question — you do not need to memorise it. What you do need to do is interpret the resulting value using the same thresholds above: \(|r_s| \geq 0.6\) = strong, \(0.2 \leq |r_s| < 0.6\) = weak, \(|r_s| < 0.2\) = no correlation.

A researcher finds a Spearman's rank correlation coefficient of \(-0.72\) between students' daily screen time and their reading test scores.

Step 1: Direction — the value is negative, so this is a negative correlation. As screen time increases, reading scores tend to decrease.

Step 2: Strength — \(|-0.72| = 0.72\), which is \(\geq 0.6\), so this is a strong negative correlation.

Step 3: Causation caution — this does not prove that screen time causes lower reading scores. Other factors (e.g. time available for reading, parental education) might explain both variables.
lessons.exam_tip_html: On ‘Compare in Context’ and ‘Describe’ questions about scatter graphs or correlation coefficients, always (1) state the direction (positive/negative/zero) and (2) state the strength using the correct threshold (strong if \(|r| \geq 0.6\), weak if \(0.2 \leq |r| < 0.6\)). Then interpret in context — what does this mean for the specific variables? The single most common error is using the word “causes” instead of “associated with” — this loses a mark on any question that rewards knowledge of the correlation/causation distinction.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Correlation describes the direction (positive, negative, zero) and strength (strong, weak, none) of the relationship between two variables. Strength thresholds: strong if \(|r| \geq 0.6\), weak if \(0.2 \leq |r| < 0.6\), no correlation if \(|r| < 0.2\).
  • Interpolation (estimating within the data range) is more reliable than extrapolation (estimating beyond it) — the relationship seen in the data may not continue outside the observed range.
  • Correlation does not imply causation — a strong association between two variables may be explained by a third lurking variable that influences both. Always consider alternative explanations before claiming a causal link.

practice_questions.text:
A researcher calculates a correlation coefficient of -0.72 between daily hours of exercise and reported stress levels.
Which statement best describes this relationship?
A) Strong positive correlation: as exercise increases, stress increases.
B) Weak negative correlation: as exercise increases, stress decreases slightly.
C) Strong negative correlation: as exercise increases, stress tends to decrease.
D) No correlation: there is no relationship between exercise and stress.
practice_questions.marks: C [1 mark] — The value is -0.72; since |-0.72| = 0.72 which is >= 0.6, this is a strong negative correlation.

practice_questions.text:
A scatter graph shows the relationship between the age of a car (in years) and its second-hand value (in pounds). The data covers cars between 1 and 8 years old.
A student uses the line of best fit to estimate the value of a 12-year-old car.
State whether this is interpolation or extrapolation, and give one reason why the estimate may be unreliable.
practice_questions.marks:
Extrapolation [1 mark] because 12 years is beyond the range of the original data (1 to 8 years) [1 mark].
Note: any valid reason for unreliability accepted, e.g. the rate of depreciation may change for very old cars.

practice_questions.text: Describe the relationship shown by a scatter graph where the points form a tight cluster close to a straight line sloping downward from left to right.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark per valid point, up to 3 marks.
- The correlation is negative: as the x-variable increases, the y-variable decreases [1].
- The correlation is strong: the points cluster closely around the line of best fit [1].
- Context-linked interpretation [1]: the pattern suggests that higher values of x are associated with lower values of y in this dataset (accept any contextual comment referencing direction and proximity of points).

practice_questions.text:
A news report claims: 'Research shows that children who eat more fish have higher reading ages — eating fish boosts brain development.'
Explain why this conclusion about causation may not be justified, referring to the concept of a lurking variable in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 2 marks per developed point, up to 4 marks.
Mastering: Two distinct reasons, each developed.
- Correlation does not imply causation [1]: even if there is a strong positive correlation between fish consumption and reading age, this does not mean fish causes higher reading ages [1].
- A lurking variable could explain both [1]: for example, wealthier families may both eat more fish (due to cost) and invest more in literacy resources (books, tutoring), making it appear that fish predicts reading age when the underlying cause is family wealth [1].
Secure: One developed point about causation with a partial example.
Developing: States 'there could be other factors' without naming or explaining a lurking variable.
Emerging: Says the correlation is not proof without explaining why.

practice_questions.text:
A study finds a Spearman's rank correlation coefficient of 0.45 between students' enjoyment ratings of a subject and their attendance rate.
Suggest and justify whether this finding provides strong enough evidence to conclude that enjoyment causes better attendance.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark for classifying the correlation and up to 4 marks for a justified evaluation.
Mastering: Correct classification, explanation of what it means, and a justified judgement on causation.
- r_s = 0.45; |0.45| is between 0.2 and 0.6, so this is a weak positive correlation [1].
- A weak correlation means the association is not consistent enough to draw firm conclusions [1].
- The finding does not provide strong enough evidence that enjoyment causes better attendance [1] because correlation does not imply causation — there could be lurking variables (e.g. teacher quality, school culture) that affect both enjoyment and attendance [1].
- A stronger correlation and/or a controlled experiment would be needed before a causal claim could be made [1].
Secure: Correct classification with partial evaluation.
Developing: Classifies but does not address causation.
Emerging: States 'it is only a correlation' without development.

practice_questions.text: Discuss whether a high value of a correlation coefficient is sufficient evidence to conclude that two variables are causally linked. Use examples to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 6 marks for a balanced discussion with examples and a judgement.
Mastering: Arguments for (strong correlation is suggestive) and against (lurking variables, correlation/causation distinction), with examples and a final judgement.
- For: a high correlation coefficient (e.g. r = 0.9) suggests a strong, consistent pattern that would be unlikely by chance [1+1].
- Against: correlation does not imply causation — e.g. there is a strong correlation between ice cream sales and drowning incidents, but hot weather (a lurking variable) explains both [1+1].
- Against: even a very high correlation between two variables could be a coincidence in a small sample [1+1].
- Judgement: a high correlation coefficient provides suggestive evidence worth investigating further, but establishing causation requires a controlled experiment or other methods that eliminate alternative explanations [1].
Secure: Two threads developed with examples.
Developing: One thread with a relevant example.
Emerging: States 'correlation is not causation' without development.

lessons.title: Reading Skew, Outliers and Distributions
lessons.description: Identifying positive and negative skew, commenting on outliers, and recognising binomial and Normal distributions.
lessons.content_html:
What Is a Distribution?

When you collect a set of data, the values spread across a range. The way those values are spread — which values are common, which are rare, whether the data clusters symmetrically or leans to one side — is the distribution of the data. Reading the shape of a distribution is a core interpretation skill: it tells you whether the data is symmetric, skewed, or has unusual values at the extremes.

Symmetrical Distributions

A symmetrical distribution is balanced — the left and right sides are roughly mirror images of each other. In a perfectly symmetrical distribution, the mean, median, and mode are all equal and sit at the centre. A classic symmetrical shape is the bell curve, which you will encounter later in this lesson when looking at the Normal distribution.

Positive Skew

A positively skewed distribution has a longer tail on the right. Most values cluster at the lower end of the scale, with a few unusually high values stretching the tail to the right. Because those extreme high values pull the mean upwards, the mean is greater than the median in a positively skewed distribution.

A real-world example: household income in the UK is positively skewed. Most households earn in a moderate range, but a small number of very high earners stretch the tail. The mean income is pulled upwards by these high earners, making it higher than the median. This is why the median is often a more representative average for income data.

Negative Skew

A negatively skewed distribution has a longer tail on the left. Most values cluster at the higher end of the scale, with a few unusually low values stretching the tail to the left. The mean is pulled downwards by those extreme low values, making it less than the median.

A real-world example: scores on an easy test might show negative skew. Most students score highly (the cluster is on the right), but a small number of students who struggled pull the tail to the left. The mean score would be lower than the median because of those very low scores.

Key Fact

Positive skew: tail on the right, mean > median. Negative skew: tail on the left, mean < median. A useful memory trick: the skew is named after the direction of the TAIL, not the main cluster.

Key Fact

Positive skew: tail on the right, mean > median. Negative skew: tail on the left, mean < median. Symmetrical: mean = median. Remember: the skew is named after the direction of the TAIL, not where the main cluster sits.

Commenting on Outliers

An outlier is a value that stands apart from the rest of the data — either much larger or much smaller than typical. Outliers can arise from genuine extreme values (a student who scored 100% on a test where everyone else scored between 40% and 80%), measurement errors (a data entry typo turning 160 cm into 16 cm), or a genuinely different subgroup in the data.

When commenting on outliers in exam questions, you should: (1) identify the outlier by referring to its approximate value, (2) suggest whether it might be a genuine extreme value or a possible error, and (3) comment on its effect on any averages you have calculated. An outlier pulls the mean towards it but does not affect the median.

Students often say “positive skew has most values on the positive side of the graph.” This is wrong. Positive skew is named after the direction of the TAIL, not where the main cluster sits. In a positively skewed distribution, the TAIL goes right (in the positive direction) and the CLUSTER sits at the lower end.

A quick check: if someone earned the most money in a room, are they pulling the mean income up? Yes — so income data is likely positively skewed (long right tail, even though most people cluster at lower incomes). That is positive skew.

Binomial Distribution (Higher)

A binomial distribution describes the number of successes in a fixed number of independent trials, where each trial has the same probability of success. The word “binomial” will appear in your exam. The key characteristics are:

  • A fixed number of trials (e.g. flipping a coin 5 times).
  • Each trial has only two possible outcomes (success or failure).
  • The probability of success is constant across all trials.
  • The trials are independent of each other.

In your exam, the number of trials \(n\) will be no greater than 5. The distribution is symmetric when the probability of success is 0.5, and skewed when the probability is not 0.5. You do not need to use formal notation for the binomial distribution — describing its characteristics in words is sufficient.

The Normal Distribution and the 68/95 Rule (Higher)

The Normal distribution is a symmetric, bell-shaped distribution where values cluster around the mean and become progressively rarer further away. It describes many real-world characteristics: the heights of adults, birth weights, exam scores, and measurement errors all tend to follow approximately Normal distributions.

The specification requires you to know two key results about the Normal distribution:

  • Approximately 68% of the data lies within one standard deviation of the mean.
  • Approximately 95% of the data lies within two standard deviations of the mean.
  • Values more than three standard deviations from the mean are very unusual.

Action and Warning Lines in Quality Assurance (Higher)

In manufacturing and quality control, products are sampled regularly to check they meet a standard. The Normal distribution is used to set warning lines (at two standard deviations from the target) and action lines (at three standard deviations from the target). If a sample mean falls outside the action lines, the production process is stopped and investigated, because such a result would be very unusual if the process were running correctly.

Standardising Data (Higher)

To compare values from two different distributions (e.g. a student's score in Maths and their score in English, which have different means and standard deviations), you can standardise by converting each value to a z-score: $$z = \frac{x - \bar{x}}{s}$$ where \(x\) is the value, \(\bar{x}\) is the mean, and \(s\) is the standard deviation. The formula will be given in the question. A z-score tells you how many standard deviations above or below the mean a value lies, allowing fair comparison across different scales.

The heights of a group of adults are Normally distributed with a mean of 170 cm and a standard deviation of 8 cm.

Within one standard deviation (162 cm to 178 cm): approximately 68% of adults. Within two standard deviations (154 cm to 186 cm): approximately 95% of adults. Heights above 194 cm or below 146 cm (three standard deviations away) are very unusual.
lessons.exam_tip_html: On questions asking you to describe or identify skew, always name the direction (“positive skew” or “negative skew”) AND describe the tail direction (“the tail stretches to the right”). For Higher questions about the Normal distribution and the 68/95 rule, show your working clearly: write out the calculation \( ext{mean} \pm 2 imes ext{standard deviation}\) before stating the range. On outlier questions, always comment on its effect on the mean compared to the median — this is frequently the second mark in a two-mark question.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Positive skew has a longer tail on the right (mean > median); negative skew has a longer tail on the left (mean < median); a symmetrical distribution has mean = median. The skew is named for the direction of the tail.
  • Outliers stand far apart from the main cluster, may be genuine extreme values or data errors, and pull the mean towards them without affecting the median.
  • Higher: the Normal distribution follows the 68/95 rule (68% within one standard deviation, 95% within two). Values more than three standard deviations from the mean are very unusual — this forms the basis of action and warning lines in quality control.

practice_questions.text:
The ages at which a group of people bought their first car are recorded. The distribution is positively skewed.
Which of the following statements about the mean and median is correct?
A) Mean < Median
B) Mean = Median
C) Mean > Median
D) The relationship between mean and median cannot be determined from skew alone.
practice_questions.marks: C [1 mark] — In a positively skewed distribution, the long right tail pulls the mean above the median.

practice_questions.text:
A dataset of 15 students' test scores is: 45, 48, 50, 51, 52, 53, 54, 55, 56, 58, 59, 60, 61, 62, 95.
The score of 95 appears to be an outlier.
Work out the mean and median of the dataset, and comment on the effect of the outlier on each.
practice_questions.marks:
Mean = (sum of all values) / 15. Sum = 45+48+50+51+52+53+54+55+56+58+59+60+61+62+95 = 859. Mean = 859/15 = 57.27 (accept 57.3) [1 mark].
Median = 8th value when ordered = 55 [1 mark].
Comment (for context): the outlier of 95 pulls the mean upwards (from approximately 55 to 57.3) but does not affect the median.

practice_questions.text:
A student looks at the following description of a distribution: 'Most values are clustered at the higher end of the scale, with a few very low values stretching the tail in the opposite direction.'
Describe the shape of this distribution, including the direction of the skew and the relative positions of the mean and median.
practice_questions.marks:
The distribution is negatively skewed [1].
The tail stretches to the left [1].
The mean is less than the median because the few low values pull the mean downwards [1].

practice_questions.text:
A production line fills packets of crisps with a target weight of 150 g. The weights are Normally distributed with a standard deviation of 4 g.
Calculate the range within which approximately 95% of packet weights will fall, and explain the significance of a packet weighing 162 g.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Calculation correct and explanation developed; Secure: Calculation correct with partial explanation.
95% range: mean +/- 2 standard deviations = 150 +/- 8 g = 142 g to 158 g [2 marks].
162 g is more than 3 standard deviations above the mean (150 + 3*4 = 162 g exactly) [1].
This is very unusual for a correctly running process and would trigger an investigation; it would fall outside the action line [1].

practice_questions.text:
A factory sets warning lines at two standard deviations from the target mean and action lines at three standard deviations. Samples are taken hourly.
Suggest and justify what the factory quality manager should do if three consecutive sample means fall between the warning line and the action line.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark per suggestion and 1 mark per justification, up to 5 marks.
Mastering: A specific action and a justified reason linked to the statistical meaning of the warning/action lines.
- Monitor the process more closely or increase the sampling frequency [1] because three consecutive means between the warning and action lines suggests a trend away from the target, even though no individual result has crossed the action line [1].
- Investigate possible causes of drift (e.g. machine calibration, raw material variability) [1] before the means cross the action line and production needs to be stopped [1].
- Record and document the values so that patterns can be identified [1]; a sustained pattern of values above the warning line (even if none crosses the action line) is a known warning sign in quality control practice [1].
Secure: One specific action with a justified reason.
Developing: Names an action without justification.
Emerging: States 'do something' without specifying what.

practice_questions.text:
The scores in a maths test have a mean of 62 and a standard deviation of 12. The scores in an English test have a mean of 55 and a standard deviation of 8. A student scores 74 in maths and 71 in English.
Discuss in which subject the student performed better relative to their peers, using standardised scores in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 6 marks for a calculation, interpretation, comparison, and judgement.
Mastering: Both z-scores calculated correctly, interpreted, compared, and a judgement made.
- Maths z-score: (74 - 62) / 12 = 12/12 = 1.0 [1]. This means the maths score is 1 standard deviation above the mean [1].
- English z-score: (71 - 55) / 8 = 16/8 = 2.0 [1]. This means the English score is 2 standard deviations above the mean [1].
- Comparison: the student performed better relative to peers in English (z = 2.0) than in maths (z = 1.0), despite scoring lower in absolute terms [1].
- Judgement: the standardised score accounts for the different difficulty levels and spread of scores in each subject, making it a fairer comparison than comparing raw marks [1].
Secure: Both z-scores correct with interpretation.
Developing: One z-score calculated with partial interpretation.
Emerging: Compares raw scores only without standardising.

glossary_terms.definition: The pattern of how values in a dataset are spread, showing which values occur frequently and which occur rarely.
A distribution where the left and right sides are roughly mirror images of each other, with the mean, median and mode all at the centre.
A distribution with a longer tail on the right-hand side, where most values are clustered at the lower end and a few high values pull the mean above the median.
A distribution with a longer tail on the left-hand side, where most values are clustered at the higher end and a few low values pull the mean below the median.
A data value that lies far away from the main cluster of values in a dataset.
A probability distribution that arises when counting the number of successes in a fixed number of independent trials, each with the same probability of success.
A symmetric, bell-shaped probability distribution where most values cluster near the mean and become increasingly rare further from the mean.
Lines on a quality control chart set at two standard deviations from the target mean; a value outside these lines suggests the process may need monitoring.
Lines on a quality control chart set at three standard deviations from the target mean; a value outside these lines indicates the process should be stopped and investigated.

lessons.title: Time Series, Trends and Rates of Change
lessons.description: Spotting trends and seasonal patterns over time, and using rates of change and index numbers in real contexts.
lessons.content_html:
What Is a Time Series?

A time series is data recorded at successive time points — monthly sales figures, quarterly unemployment rates, annual birth rates. Plotting these values against time produces a time series graph (sometimes called a line chart) that lets you see patterns that would be invisible in a table of numbers.

Trends

The trend is the overall direction a time series is heading in the long run, ignoring short-term ups and downs. A trend might be rising (e.g. average house prices in the UK over decades), falling (e.g. infant mortality rates over the last century), or roughly constant. Identifying the trend is the first step in interpreting a time series.

It is important to distinguish the trend from short-term variation. A shop’s weekly sales might spike before Christmas and dip in January, but the underlying trend over several years might be consistently rising. The trend is what you would see if you smoothed out the seasonal bumps.

Key Fact

A trend is the long-term overall direction. A seasonal pattern is a regular, repeating short-term fluctuation at the same time each year (or each cycle). Both can be present in the same time series.

Seasonal and Cyclic Trends

A seasonal trend is a regular, repeating pattern tied to the time of year. Ice cream sales peak in summer and fall in winter every year; gas and electricity consumption peaks in winter every year; retail sales peak before Christmas every year. These patterns are predictable and expected.

A cyclic trend is similar but not tied to a fixed calendar period — it represents a pattern that rises and falls over a longer, less regular time scale (such as economic business cycles that might last several years). The specification uses the term “cyclic” as well as “seasonal” and you should be able to interpret both.

When a question asks you to use a seasonal or cyclic trend to make a prediction, always say: “Based on the seasonal pattern in the data, I would expect [variable] to [rise/fall] in [period] because [reason from the pattern].” Predictions based on time series should acknowledge that the pattern may not continue indefinitely.

Rates of Change

A rate of change expresses how quickly something changes over time. Rather than just showing the raw count, a rate puts change in proportion — allowing meaningful comparison between populations of different sizes or time periods of different lengths.

The specification covers several specific rate measures used in real UK contexts. These include the birth rate (number of live births per 1,000 people per year), the death rate (number of deaths per 1,000 people per year), house price change, and unemployment rates. All rate-of-change formulae will be given in the question — you will not be asked to recall them from memory. What matters is reading the formula carefully and applying it correctly to the data given.

A larger country has more births per year than a smaller one, simply because it has more people. Comparing raw birth counts tells you little. The birth rate (births per 1,000 population) corrects for population size, allowing a fair comparison between countries or regions of different sizes.

Similarly, a rise in the number of deaths does not necessarily mean mortality is worsening — the population may have grown or aged. The death rate puts this in proportion. Always use rates when comparing populations of different sizes.

Index Numbers

Index numbers express a value relative to a chosen base period (usually set to 100). Instead of quoting actual prices or quantities, an index shows how much a value has changed from the base. If the base year has an index of 100 and a later year has an index of 115, then the value has risen by 15% from the base.

UK economists and statisticians use three important index numbers that you should know by name:

  • RPI (Retail Price Index): Measures changes in the average price of a basket of goods and services purchased by households. Published monthly by the ONS. Used for uprating certain benefits, wages, and rail fares.
  • CPI (Consumer Price Index): Similar to RPI but uses a different methodology and basket of goods. The Bank of England uses CPI as its target measure for inflation.
  • GDP (Gross Domestic Product): Measures the total economic output of a country. GDP index tracks growth or contraction of the economy over time.
Key Fact

RPI and CPI both measure price inflation, with RPI and CPI differing in methodology. GDP measures total economic output. All three are published by UK government bodies and used in policy decisions. All rate-of-change formulae are given in the exam — focus on reading and applying them, not memorising them.

Calculating Rates of Change (Higher)

At Higher tier, you will be asked to calculate rates of change from tables using a formula that is given in the question. Typical examples include: calculating a birth rate from a table of births and population figures, or calculating a percentage change in house price from year-to-year data.

The key skill is identifying the right values to substitute into the formula. Read the column headers carefully to identify which values go where. State your working clearly and give your answer in the correct units (rates are usually expressed per 1,000 or as a percentage).

Weighted Index Numbers (Higher)

A weighted index number assigns different weights to different items based on their importance in a typical household’s spending. For example, if a family spends 40% of its budget on housing and 5% on entertainment, housing gets a much larger weight in the index. A simple (unweighted) average of all price changes would understate the effect of rising housing costs on the household’s total bill.

The CPI and RPI are both weighted indices. The formula for a weighted index will be given in the question. Your task is to apply it correctly: multiply each item’s price relative by its weight, sum these products, and divide by the sum of the weights.

When asked to interpret a time series graph in the exam, work through these steps:

  • State the overall trend — is it rising, falling, or steady over the period shown?
  • Identify any seasonal pattern — is there a regular peak and trough that repeats each year or cycle?
  • Note any unusual features — a sudden spike or dip that breaks the trend; is there a plausible real-world explanation?
  • Quantify where possible — “the value rose from approximately 40 to 65 between 2010 and 2020” is better than “it went up.”
lessons.exam_tip_html: On ‘Describe’ questions about time series graphs, the most common error is describing what the graph looks like (“the line goes up and down”) rather than what it shows about the data (“sales rose steadily from around 120,000 to 180,000 units between 2015 and 2020, with a seasonal dip each January”). Always include the trend direction, specific values or time periods, and any seasonal pattern. On rate-of-change calculation questions, read the formula in the question carefully before substituting values — do not guess the formula from memory.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • A time series has a trend (the long-term direction) and may also have a seasonal pattern (a regular, repeating fluctuation). Both must be described when interpreting a time series graph, with specific values where possible.
  • Rates of change (birth rate, death rate, house price change) put raw counts in proportion for fair comparison. All formulae are given in the question — focus on reading and applying them correctly.
  • Index numbers (RPI, CPI, GDP) express values relative to a base period (= 100). Weighted index numbers assign different weights to items based on their importance in typical spending — unweighted averages would overstate or understate the impact of price changes on household budgets.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following best describes a seasonal trend in a time series?
A) A gradual long-term increase in the values over many years.
B) A one-off sudden spike caused by an unusual event.
C) A regular, repeating pattern at the same time each year.
D) A random variation with no discernible pattern.
practice_questions.marks: C [1 mark] — A seasonal trend is a regular, repeating pattern tied to the same time of year.

practice_questions.text:
A country recorded 620,000 births in a year when its population was 62,000,000.
The formula for birth rate is: Birth rate = (number of births / total population) x 1000.
Calculate the birth rate, giving your answer to one decimal place.
practice_questions.marks: Birth rate = (620,000 / 62,000,000) x 1000 = 0.01 x 1000 = 10.0 births per 1,000 population [2 marks; award 1 mark for correct substitution into the formula].

practice_questions.text:
A time series graph shows monthly electricity consumption for a household over three years. The overall values are slowly rising, but each January shows a noticeably higher reading than the surrounding months.
Describe the trend and the seasonal pattern visible in this time series.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark per point, up to 3 marks.
- Overall trend: electricity consumption is rising slowly over the three-year period [1].
- Seasonal pattern: consumption peaks each January and is lower in the warmer months (suggesting higher winter usage, likely due to heating and longer darkness) [1].
- The January peaks are regular and repeating, occurring at the same time each year [1].

practice_questions.text: Explain why the RPI and CPI are described as weighted index numbers, and why weighting is important for measuring the impact of price changes on household budgets.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 2 marks per developed point, up to 4 marks.
Mastering: What weighting means and why it matters for households.
- Weighted index numbers assign different weights to different items based on how much households typically spend on each [1]; for example, housing costs receive a larger weight than entertainment because households spend more of their budget on housing [1].
- Without weighting, a large price rise in a minor item (e.g. bus fares) would have the same effect on the index as a large price rise in a major item (e.g. food) [1]; weighting ensures the index reflects changes in the things households actually spend most money on [1].
Secure: One developed point about weighting.
Developing: States that weighting is used without explaining why.
Emerging: Names RPI or CPI without addressing the weighting concept.

practice_questions.text:
An economist uses a time series of house prices to extrapolate prices 10 years into the future.
Suggest and justify two reasons why this extrapolation may be unreliable.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark per reason and 1 mark per justification, up to 5 marks.
Mastering: Two reasons, each with a justification linking to a specific feature of time series extrapolation.
- The past trend may not continue [1]; economic conditions (interest rates, housing policy, global events) can shift the trend direction in ways that are impossible to predict 10 years ahead, so the extrapolated line may diverge significantly from actual prices [1].
- Seasonal effects compound over time [1]; even small seasonal fluctuations accumulate over 10 years of extrapolation, making point estimates increasingly unreliable as the prediction horizon extends [1].
- The time series itself may contain outliers or one-off events (e.g. a financial crash) [1]; if such events influenced the trend line used for extrapolation, the forecast inherits these distortions [1].
Secure: Two reasons, one justified.
Developing: One reason with a justification.
Emerging: States 'the future is uncertain' without specifying why the time series makes it unreliable.

practice_questions.text:
Two countries both report that their birth rate has fallen over the last 20 years. Country A has a population of 5 million; Country B has a population of 150 million.
Discuss whether comparing their birth rates is a more meaningful approach than comparing their total numbers of births.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 6 marks for a balanced discussion with examples and a judgement.
Mastering: Arguments for using rates, acknowledgement of limitations, and a judgement.
- Comparing total births is misleading because Country B will always have far more births simply because it has 30 times more people [1+1].
- Birth rates (births per 1,000 population) control for population size, allowing a fairer comparison of the actual fertility patterns in each country [1+1].
- Rates are more useful for policy purposes: a government wants to know whether the share of new births is declining relative to population size, not just the absolute number [1+1].
- Limitation: birth rates do not capture age structure differences — a country with a very young population will have a higher birth rate even at the same fertility per woman [1].
- Judgement: comparing birth rates is generally more meaningful than raw counts when populations differ in size, but further context (age structure, immigration) is still needed for full interpretation [1].
Secure: Two threads developed.
Developing: One thread with a relevant example.
Emerging: States 'use a rate' without explaining why.

knowledge_checks.q: What does the trend in a time series describe?
options: A regular repeating pattern at the same time each year
A sudden one-off spike in the data
The overall long-term direction of the data, ignoring short-term fluctuations
The difference between the highest and lowest values recorded

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following is an example of a seasonal pattern in a time series?
options: House prices rising slowly every year over a decade
A factory closing permanently in one year

GDP growing steadily for five consecutive years

Match each index to what it measures:

Changes in consumer prices used as the Bank of England's inflation target
Total economic output of a country

glossary_terms.definition: A sequence of data values recorded at successive points in time, used to identify trends, seasonal patterns, and changes over time.
The overall long-term direction of a time series, ignoring short-term fluctuations.
A regular, repeating pattern in a time series that occurs at the same time of year (or same stage of a regular cycle) every year.
A measure of how much a quantity changes per unit of time or per unit of population, calculated from a given formula.
Numbers that express the value of a quantity relative to a base period value, set to 100, enabling comparison over time.
An index number that gives different items in the basket different weights according to their importance in typical household spending.

lessons.title: The Statistical Enquiry Cycle: Reviewing the Whole Investigation
lessons.description: Linking all five stages of the Statistical Enquiry Cycle, then critiquing a fictional investigation.
lessons.content_html:
This lesson covers the general principles of the Statistical Enquiry Cycle that apply to all students. The specific investigation, data and methods your class used in your coursework or class project will be different — refer to your teacher's notes alongside this lesson.

The Statistical Enquiry Cycle

Statistics is not just a collection of techniques — it is a systematic way of answering questions about the world. The Statistical Enquiry Cycle (SEC) is the overarching framework that ties all the individual techniques together. Each of your two exam papers ends with a question that integrates all five stages of the SEC, so understanding the cycle thoroughly is essential.

The five stages are:

  • Stage 1: Initial Planning — Define a question or hypothesis to investigate. Decide what data to collect, how to collect and record it, and how to process and represent it. Justify each decision.
  • Stage 2: Data Collection — Collect the data using the chosen method (primary or secondary). Recognise constraints, acknowledge sources, and be aware of sensitivity issues.
  • Stage 3: Data Processing and Presentation — Organise and clean the data. Choose appropriate graphs and statistical measures. Use technology to automate processing where appropriate.
  • Stage 4: Interpretation of Results — Analyse diagrams and calculations. Draw conclusions that relate back to the original question or hypothesis. Make inferences or predictions and discuss reliability.
  • Stage 5: Evaluation and Review — Identify weaknesses in approach or representation. Suggest improvements. Refine the process to investigate further.
Key Fact

The five stages of the SEC: (1) Initial Planning, (2) Data Collection, (3) Data Processing and Presentation, (4) Interpretation of Results, (5) Evaluation and Review. Both exam papers end with a SEC question that tests your ability to link all five stages.

Stage 1 in Detail: Initial Planning

Good planning makes all subsequent stages easier. At Stage 1, you must define a testable hypothesis, decide what data you need (and why), choose your sampling method (and justify it), and plan how you will process the data. Decisions made at this stage affect every other stage. A vague hypothesis leads to ambiguous data; a biased sampling method undermines any conclusion.

Stage 4 in Detail: Interpretation of Results

Interpretation is where your statistics turn into meaning. You must analyse the graphs and measures you calculated, reach conclusions that relate to your original question, and discuss the reliability of your findings. Conclusions must be in context — not “the mean is higher” but “students who revised more than five hours scored higher on average, with a mean of 72% compared to 58% for those who revised fewer than two hours.”

Reliability of findings depends on several factors: the size of the sample, how representative it is, whether the data collection method was valid, and whether there are alternative explanations for the pattern seen. Always consider: could a lurking variable explain this result? Could sampling bias have inflated or deflated the finding?

Stage 5 in Detail: Evaluation and Review

Evaluation is not about listing everything that went well — it is about identifying specific weaknesses and suggesting specific improvements. The examiner wants to see that you understand why a weakness matters, not just that something could have been done differently.

The structure that scores highest in evaluation questions: (1) identify a weakness at a specific SEC stage, (2) explain why that weakness undermines the conclusion, (3) suggest a specific improvement. This three-part structure applies whether you are evaluating a fictional enquiry or your own class investigation.

The 8-mark SEC Critique question (one of the highest-mark questions in each paper) presents a fictional investigation scenario and asks you to evaluate it. The structure that scores Mastering is:

Step 1: Identify a weakness at one SEC stage (e.g. Stage 2 — Data Collection: “The investigator used opportunity sampling from one shopping centre.”)

Step 2: Explain why this weakness undermines the conclusion: “This means the sample is likely biased towards shoppers at that location, who may differ systematically in their habits from the wider population. The conclusion therefore cannot be generalised.”

Step 3: Suggest a specific improvement: “A stratified random sample drawn from a complete sample frame of the target population would reduce this bias.”

Step 4: Repeat for a second SEC stage (e.g. Stage 1 — Planning: “The hypothesis is vague and does not specify measurable variables.”)

Mastering responses identify weaknesses at TWO different SEC stages and follow the three-step structure for each. Students who describe what the investigation did rather than evaluate its limitations score Emerging or Developing only.

Target Audience and Communication

Stage 4 also involves communicating your findings clearly to a target audience. A report written for a school governor has different requirements from one written for a science journal. The specification expects you to consider: is the level of technical language appropriate? Are the graphs and tables clearly labelled? Do the conclusions use plain, accessible language?

Good communication means presenting conclusions clearly and concisely, using appropriate visualisations, and not overloading the reader with unnecessary technical detail. Poor communication — even when the statistics are correct — means the findings fail to reach the people who need to act on them.

Sample Size, Reliability and Replication

The specification makes an important point about sample size: replication — the ability of another researcher to reach a similar conclusion by repeating the study — is more likely when the sample is large and representative. A finding based on 10 participants is much less replicable than one based on 1,000.

A larger sample reduces the impact of random variation on the results. In a very small sample, one or two unusual respondents can dominate the findings. In a larger sample, their influence is diluted. This is why increasing sample size is one of the most commonly recommended improvements in evaluation questions.

Distribution of Sample Means (Higher)

When you take many different samples from the same population and calculate the mean of each, those sample means form their own distribution. The specification requires you to know, at an intuitive level, that a set of sample means is more closely distributed (less spread out) than the individual values from the same population. This means the mean of any given sample is a better estimate of the population mean than any single individual value from the population would be.

Why? Individual values in a population are spread widely by natural variability. But when you take a mean of several values, the high values and low values in the sample tend to cancel each other out, pulling the sample mean back towards the centre. The larger the sample, the more this cancellation effect reduces the spread of sample means.

You do not need to use any formal notation for this idea — a clear verbal explanation in context is sufficient. If asked in an exam: “The sample means form a tighter distribution than the individual values because extreme values within each sample cancel out when averaged.”

The most common reason for losing marks in SEC evaluation questions is describing rather than evaluating. Describing says: “The investigator used opportunity sampling.” Evaluating says: “The use of opportunity sampling means the sample over-represents people who visit shopping centres, which may differ from the wider population in their habits — so the conclusions cannot be generalised.”

Every evaluation point needs three parts: (1) what the weakness is, (2) why it matters for the conclusion, (3) what specific change would fix it. Missing any of these parts limits your mark to Developing at best.

Key Fact

Evaluation structure for full marks: (1) identify the weakness at a named SEC stage, (2) explain why it undermines the conclusion, (3) suggest a specific, actionable improvement. Use this structure for both weaknesses in an 8-mark question.
lessons.exam_tip_html: The 8-mark SEC Critique question is one of the most consistently under-performed questions in each paper. The examiner report repeatedly notes that students describe the investigation rather than evaluate it. The difference: describing says what was done; evaluating says why it is a problem and how to fix it. Structure every weakness as: (1) name the stage and the weakness, (2) explain the impact on the conclusion, (3) suggest a specific improvement. Aim for two such weaknesses at two different SEC stages to access the top mark band.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Statistical Enquiry Cycle has five stages — Initial Planning, Data Collection, Data Processing and Presentation, Interpretation of Results, and Evaluation and Review — and the SEC question at the end of each paper integrates all five.
  • Conclusions must be context-based, referring to specific values and the original hypothesis. Reliability depends on sample size, representativeness, and the validity of the data collection method.
  • Evaluation scores highest when it identifies a weakness at a specific SEC stage, explains why it undermines the conclusion, and suggests a specific improvement — not just a vague comment that something “could be better.”

practice_questions.text:
Which stage of the Statistical Enquiry Cycle involves deciding what data to collect and choosing a sampling method?
A) Interpretation of Results
B) Data Processing and Presentation
C) Evaluation and Review
D) Initial Planning
practice_questions.marks: D [1 mark] — Initial Planning involves defining the hypothesis and deciding how data will be collected and processed.

practice_questions.text:
A student investigates whether students who eat breakfast score higher on memory tests than those who skip breakfast. She collects data and finds that breakfast eaters scored a mean of 68% versus 59% for those who skipped breakfast.
Write a conclusion for this investigation that refers to context and considers reliability.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark per valid point, up to 4 marks.
- Context-based conclusion: breakfast eaters scored higher on average (mean 68%) than students who skipped breakfast (mean 59%), suggesting a positive association between eating breakfast and memory test performance [1+1].
- Reliability consideration: the reliability of this finding depends on the sample size and how representative it is of all students [1].
- Alternative explanation / limitation: other factors (e.g. sleep quality, general health, home environment) may explain the difference, so a causal link cannot be claimed from this data alone [1].

practice_questions.text:
A research team investigated whether physical activity levels in adults vary by age group. They asked people at a leisure centre to complete a questionnaire.
Describe one weakness in their data collection method and explain how it affects the reliability of their conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark for identifying the weakness and 2 marks for explaining its impact.
Weakness: sampling at a leisure centre is opportunity sampling and will over-represent people who already participate in physical activity [1].
Explanation: this introduces systematic bias into the sample — the people least likely to exercise (e.g. sedentary adults) are excluded, meaning the physical activity levels recorded will be higher than those of the general adult population, making the conclusions unrepresentative [1+1].

practice_questions.text:
Suggest and justify two improvements to the following investigation design.

An online survey investigating daily social media use was posted on three social media platforms. 300 responses were collected over one week.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark per improvement and 1 mark per justification linked to a specific problem, up to 5 marks.
Mastering: Two specific improvements, each justified with reference to a named bias or reliability issue.
- Change the data collection method to a stratified random sample using a sample frame [1]; collecting data only from people who use the specific social media platforms surveyed excludes non-users (the group most likely to have low social media use), severely biasing the results upwards [1].
- Extend the data collection period and vary the time of day [1]; collecting over only one week may miss weekly patterns (e.g. heavier weekend use) and people who check social media at different times may be excluded [1].
- Ask participants about their actual usage data (screen time from phone settings) rather than self-reporting [1]; self-reported social media use is prone to recall bias and social desirability bias, reducing the validity of the data [1].
Secure: Two improvements, one justified.
Developing: One improvement with a justification.
Emerging: Names a change without justifying it.

practice_questions.text: Explain why larger sample sizes generally lead to more reliable findings, making reference to the distribution of sample means in your answer. (Higher)
practice_questions.marks:
Award 2 marks per developed point, up to 4 marks.
Mastering: Two distinct reasons, the second linking to the distribution of sample means.
- A larger sample reduces the influence of random variation [1]; one or two unusually high or low values in a small sample can dominate the mean, but in a larger sample their effect is diluted by the other values [1].
- A set of sample means from larger samples is more closely distributed around the true population mean than a set of sample means from smaller samples [1]; this means that any individual sample mean is a more reliable estimate of the population mean when the sample is large [1].
Secure: One developed point.
Developing: States 'larger samples are more reliable' without explaining why.
Emerging: Confuses sample size with sample representativeness.

practice_questions.text:
Read the following investigation description and answer the question below.

A Year 11 student investigated whether school canteen food quality affects student performance. She asked 20 students from her form class to rate canteen food quality on a scale of 1-5 and compared their ratings to their most recent test scores.

Using the structure of the Statistical Enquiry Cycle, identify a weakness at two different stages of this investigation and for each: explain why the weakness undermines the conclusions and suggest a specific improvement.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks using the three-part structure (identify/explain/suggest) for each of two SEC stages, up to 8 marks.
Mastering: Two weaknesses at two different stages, each fully developed.
Stage 1 (Initial Planning):
- Weakness: the hypothesis is not clearly defined — 'school canteen food quality affects performance' does not specify which aspect of performance or how food quality will be operationalised [1].
- Explanation: without a precise hypothesis, it is unclear what the investigation is testing. The comparison of a subjective rating to a test score may not measure what the student intends to investigate [1].
- Improvement: write a specific, testable hypothesis such as 'students who rate canteen food quality >= 4 will achieve higher mean scores on standardised maths tests than those who rate quality <= 2' [1].
Stage 2 (Data Collection):
- Weakness: the sample of 20 students from one form class is very small and uses opportunity/judgement sampling rather than random sampling [1].
- Explanation: a sample of 20 from one form class is unlikely to be representative of all students, as classmates may share similar backgrounds, diets, and study habits. The conclusions cannot be generalised to the whole school or beyond [1].
- Improvement: use a stratified random sample across all year groups and form classes to ensure the sample reflects the school population proportionally, and aim for a sample size of at least 100 [1].
Alternative valid stages include Stage 3 (self-reported food ratings are subjective and not validated) and Stage 5 (the investigation compares an average over an unspecified period to one test score, which may not reflect typical performance).
Secure: Two weaknesses, both explained but not fully developed improvements.
Developing: Two weaknesses identified without developed explanations.
Emerging: Describes the investigation rather than evaluating it.

knowledge_checks.q: Which stage of the SEC involves identifying weaknesses in approach and suggesting improvements?
What does replication mean in the context of a statistical investigation?
options: Repeating calculations to check for arithmetic errors
The ability of another researcher to reach a similar conclusion by repeating the study on a different sample
Using the same data to produce two different types of graph
Running the investigation with twice the original sample size

knowledge_checks.q: The SEC question in both exam papers requires you to identify a weakness at _____ different stages of the cycle for full marks.
At Stage 4 of the SEC, conclusions must refer back to the original _____ and be stated in context, not just as numerical observations.
Match each SEC stage to the key activity that occurs at that stage:
right: Define a testable hypothesis and decide how data will be collected
Apply sampling methods, acknowledging sources and constraints
Identify weaknesses and suggest specific improvements

flashcard_questions.q: What three things does a high-scoring evaluation response include?

flashcard_questions.q: Why does a larger sample size improve reliability?

flashcard_questions.a: The ability of another researcher to reach a similar conclusion by repeating the study on a different sample.
flashcard_questions.q: What is replication in statistics?

flashcard_questions.a: The specific group of people for whom the statistical report or findings are intended.
flashcard_questions.q: What is the target audience in statistical communication?

flashcard_questions.a: Numbers without context have no meaning for the question being investigated; the spec requires interpretation linked to the original hypothesis.
flashcard_questions.q: Why must conclusions be context-based rather than just numerical?

flashcard_questions.a: Identifying weaknesses in the approach or representation and suggesting improvements to refine the investigation.
flashcard_questions.q: What does the specification mean by 'evaluation and review' at Stage 5?

flashcard_questions.a: Extreme values in each sample cancel out when averaged, pulling sample means towards the true population mean.
flashcard_questions.q: Why is a set of sample means less spread out than individual values from the same population? (Higher)

flashcard_questions.q: What happens to the distribution of sample means as sample size increases? (Higher)

glossary_terms.definition: The five-stage framework for conducting a statistical investigation: initial planning, data collection, data processing and presentation, interpretation of results, and evaluation and review.
The specific group of people for whom a statistical report or findings are intended.
The property of a finding that allows it to be reproduced by another researcher following the same method on a different sample from the same population.
